(a) Tumors 4 and 7 analyzed as in Fig. 1h. Cells are colored by classification or the indicated feature levels. (b) Heatmap of mean feature levels in each subpopulation across all HR+ tumors analyzed by CyTOF (n = 14, including 3 anchor repeats, see Table S3). Rows present standardized values. (c) Two luminal PDX models analyzed by CyTOF after removal of mouse cells (human CD298-positive; mouse MHC class 1-negative), and classification into three subpopulations (Fig. 1j). PDX-1 comprised of six tumors, with equal cell sampling per tumor; PDX-2 comprised of one tumor. Heatmaps show the mean feature levels within each subpopulation for each model. (d) UMAP of MCF7 CyTOF data using all measured markers. Points are colored by cluster (left) or the indicated feature or signature (right).

(a) Distribution of DBSACN-defined cell subpopulations across independent MCF7 CyTOF experiments of MCF7 cells, showing consistent proportions of the different cell states. (b) UMAP representation and DBSCAN clustering of two different MCF7 parental cells or single-cell derived clones analyzed by CyTOF, using only epigenetic features. Points are colored by the classification of different subpopulations or the expression levels of the indicated feature or signature (PermCell). (c) The distribution of cells among the populations defined by DBSCAN clustering in the MCF7 parental (p) or single-cell derived clones (c). The single-cell derived clones recapitulate the entire spectrum of heterogeneity observed in the parental population. (d) UMAP representation of CyTOF analysis of six independently grown tumors from the PDX-1 model (n = 6 tumors, each grown in a different mouse), colored by subpopulations. Cells from each individual tumor are mapped onto the joint UMAP, and the distribution of cells among the three subpopulations for each tumor is shown.

(a) Confusion matrix of XGBoost model predictions for all 3 subpopulations across HR+ tumors (n = 14) using only epigenetic features, excluding cell identity markers. Rows were normalized to show predictions as percentages of cells within each true class. (b) Representative examples of XGBoost-based noise prediction procedure. UMAPs of individual tumors are shown before (left) and after (right) prediction. Points are colored by classification; non-clustered cells before prediction, or cells in which prediction confidence <95% are marked in gray. (c-d) XGBoost models distinguishing Cycling cells from all other tumor cells (c) or specifically the basal-like cells (d) within the HR+ CyTOF cohort. SHAP scores show feature contributions to classification, ranked in descending order. (e) Percentage of proliferating cells (assessed by the levels of pRb, as in Fig. S3) in each epigenetic sub-populations (Cycling, luminal and basal-like). The basal-like and luminal sub-populations do not differ due to differences in the proliferative state. (f) The differences in the average levels of the indicated features between the basal-like and luminal sub-populations in the luminal PDX models. Basal-like cells show a recurrent pattern of both up and downregulated histone PTMs, highly similar to the pattern observed in fresh human tumors.

(a) UMAP of CyTOF data from tumors (as in Fig. S4), colored by the assigned clusters (top) or the basal-like epigenetic signature (basal PermCell score, bottom), which is derived solely from histone modifications. (b) UMAP of two MCF7 parental cultures and three single-cell-derived clones analyzed by CyTOF using only epigenetic features, colored by assigned clusters (top) or the basal-like epigenetic signature (bottom).

(a) Scatter plot comparing basal-like cell fraction with estrogen receptor (ER) positivity by IHC across tumors (n = 11). Spearman correlation coefficient and two-sided p-value are indicated. (b,c) Basal-like cell fraction in HR+ tumors stratified by progesterone receptor (PR) IHC (b; 100% PR-positive, n = 7; lower PR positivity, n = 4) or TP53 status (c; wild-type, n = 8; mutant, n = 3). Two-sided Wilcoxon tests. Boxes show median and 25th–75th percentiles; whiskers extend within 1.5xIQR. (d) Differential protein abundance between K5High and K5Low populations in tumor 19. Axes show protein intensity difference (K5High-K5Low) and -log10(p-value), respectively. Two-sided Student’s t-tests with FDR correction; Green and pink dots depict proteins significantly deregulated (Fold change>1.5, q-value < 0.05). Labeled are chromatin regulators differentially expressed between the two populations. (e) Principal component analysis (PCA) of RNA-seq profiles from sorted MCF7 subpopulations. Basal-like cells (K5High GATA3Low, n = 3), extreme luminal cells (K5Low GATA3High, n = 3), and bulk MCF7 cells (n = 2). Points represent independently sorted population. Axes indicate variance explained. (f) Differential gene expression between basal-like (K5High GATA3Low, n = 3) and bulk MCF7 cells (n = 2). Significantly upregulated (pink) and downregulated (green) genes are indicated (DESeq2, Benjamini–Hochberg-adjusted p-value < 0.05, log2FC > 1). EMT-associated genes (hallmark epithelial-mesenchymal transition gene set) are enriched among upregulated transcripts in the basal-like population and highlighted with a black outline. CD74, a membrane-bound protein upregulated in the basal-like cells, is marked in dark pink. (g) CD74 expression across basal-like (n = 3), bulk (n = 2), and extreme luminal (n = 3) MCF7 populations. Points represent independently sorted population; expression is shown as rld values. Statistical significance was derived from DESeq2 differential expression analysis with Benjamini–Hochberg correction for multiple testing. (h) Representative wound-healing assay images of sorted CD74Low and CD74High MCF7 cells at the indicated times. Three independently recovered sorted populations from the same sort were analyzed. The gap area is highlighted in green. Scale bar = 300 μm.

(a) TCGA-BRCA DNA-methylation dataset (n = 782)51 was deconvoluted into three archetypes. Dots show tumor archetype composition and colored by PAM50 subtype. The archetype V3 is associated with basal-like triple-negative tumors. The composition of archetypes within the three tumors analyzed in this study (T18, T19, and T23, highlighted) clusters with luminal breast tumors from the TCGA cohort. (b) Genes were ranked by correlation between methylation archetypes and matched TCGA-BRCA expression, followed by GSEA111 against MSigDB hallmark gene sets (Table S4b). V1 and V2 archetypes are associated with luminal transcriptional programs while V3 archetype is enriched for the EMT program. Normalized Enrichment Scores (NES) of representative terms are shown. Black outline denotes BH-adjusted p-value < 0.05. See Fig. S5a for all terms. (c-d) K5High and K5Low sorted cells from tumors 5 and 23 were subjected to enzyme-mediated methylation sequencing (EM-seq, n = 4 replicates, 200 cells/replicate), and differentially methylated gene promoters were identified. For each sample, functional enrichment analysis was performed separately for genes with hypermethylated or hypomethylated promoters. Shown are the top 10 enriched terms from the MSigDB Hallmark gene set collection (c) or a curated list of breast cancer cell identity signatures (d) with nominal p-value < 0.05 (one-sided hypergeometric test). Circle size represents the number of genes from the input list overlapping each gene set, and transparency reflects -log10(p-value). (e) A CpG-island (CGI) methylation signature distinguishing K5High and K5Low states, derived using CGIs showing concordant differential methylation between the states in both tumor 5 and 23. Shown is the projection of this signature into DNA methylation profiles from the TCGA-BRCA dataset. Positive scores indicate greater similarity to the EM-seq-derived K5High methylation program, whereas negative scores indicate similarity to the K5Low state. Boxplots show the distribution of signature scores across basal-like (n = 96) or luminal (n = 418) tumors with points representing individual tumors. Boxes show median and 25th–75th percentiles; whiskers extend to the largest/smallest value within 1.5×IQR. The K5High methylation program is enriched in basal-like breast tumors. Two-sided Mann–Whitney U test. (f) TCGA-BRCA DNA-methylation dataset deconvoluted into three archetypes as in a, with K5high and K5low-sorted populations from tumors 5 and 23 projected onto the archetype space. K5high populations are shifted toward the V3 archetype, consistent with enrichment for basal/EMT-associated methylation programs. (g) Representation of tumors from the TCGA-BRCA cohort based on the four-archetype decomposition described in Fig. 3a, colored by V1 contribution. K5high and K5low-sorted populations from tumors 5 and 23 are projected onto the UMAP embedding. K5high populations are localized to regions characterized by higher V1 contribution, consistent with the EMT-associated methylation programs.

(a) WGBS reads were clustered by DNA methylation patterns over 100 bp bins55, and each bin was scored for entropy, reflecting DNA methylation pattern heterogeneity; bins containing one pattern have zero entropy. Illustration, rows represent methylation patterns, filled/open circles indicate methylated/unmethylated CpGs and #r denotes supporting reads. Histograms show mean entropy scores of CGIs in tumor 19 (n = 17,434), tumor 18 (n = 20,845) and tumor 23 (n = 22,440). Most CGIs are unmethylated and have zero entropy scores. The intermediate and high-entropy bins are marked in pink and red. (b) Intermediate- and high-entropy CGIs (entropy>0) were linked to genes and analyzed for enrichment against MSigDB Hallmark genesets85. Pathways significantly enriched in all three tumors are shown (one-sided hypergeometric test, nominal p-value < 0.05). Dot size indicates overlapping genes; color indicates -log10(p-value). Variable CGIs are significantly enriched for genes related to EMT. (c) The Basal-luminal index was used to score the transcriptional identity of tumor cells13, and cells from each tumor were divided into quartiles; a low index score corresponds to expression of luminal identity genes (Q1) and a high index score corresponds to expression of basal-like identity genes (Q4). Cell-to-cell distance was calculated within each quartile to assess transcriptional heterogeneity; medians are shown for each sample. Bottom, representative UMAP and quartile definition for tumor 12-R. (d) Vendi score96 was used to calculate epigenetic heterogeneity within luminal or basal-like subpopulation (as defined in Figs. 1, 2, across n = 11 luminal tumors) using single-cell CyTOF histone PTMs measurements. Points show the mean across 5,000 rarefactions; error bars indicate uncertainty intervals (2.5th–97.5th percentiles) of the rarefied score distribution. Histone PTM levels are more variable in basal-like cells.

(a) UMAPs of H3K4me1 (left, n = 17,062 cells) and H3K4me3 (right, n = 12,883 cells) snCUT&Tag 50 kb bins matrices from three tumor samples (PC1 representing read counts excluded; CD45-negative cells). Shared stroma clusters are outlined. (b) UMAPs as in a, colored according to H3K4me1 or H3K4me3 enrichment over fibroblast identity genes: FAP, COL3A1 and DCN (left) or endothelial identity genes: EMCN, PECAM1 and NOTCH3 (right). Higher UCell scores indicate stronger enrichment at genes associated with the corresponding stromal identity. (c,d) H3K4me1 (c) or H3K4me3 (d) UMAPS from all three tumors (50k bins matrix), colored by cluster. The portion of cells from each tumor that constitutes the clusters is shown below. Shared clusters were classified as stroma, as verified by gene activity; Boxed tumor clusters were analyzed further. For H3K4me3, limited number of cells passed quality control thresholds for tumor 8, thus data quality for this sample is lower. (e) Genomic annotation of H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 snCUT&Tag pseudo-bulk peaks, after stoma removal. Stacked bar plots show percentage of peaks assigned to genomic features. (f) For each tumor sample, removing the stroma compartment, a scTransform-normalized H3K4me3 gene activity was generated (excluding read counts information), represented by UMAP and clustered using Louvain clustering. Cell numbers are indicated. (g) Tumor 8 H3K4me1 UMAP (Fig. 3e), colored by UCell scores derived based on the genes contributing to the enrichment of the indicated terms. Cluster 2 shows high H3K4me1 signal on genes associated with basal-like cell identity. While the EMT signature was not significantly enriched for this cluster (FDR-adjusted p-value > 0.05), the corresponding UCell score is shown for comparison using EMT-associated genes contributing to the cluster. (h) Differentially H3K4me3-bound genes identified for each cluster shown in f (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, log2FC > 1, adjusted p-value < 0.01) were tested against MSigDB Hallmark and Breast-related genesets (Table S4). Terms enriched in cluster 1 in all three tumors are shown (one-sided hypergeometric test, FDR-adjusted P < 0.05). (i) Pseudu-bulk H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 genome-browser tracks from basal-like clusters (pink) or equal numbers of cells sampled from all other clusters (green) at representative genomic regions.

(a,b) H3K4me1 or H3K4me3 reads per cell versus negative ER-signaling score in tumor 15 (a) or positive ER-signaling score in tumor 18 (b). Points represent cells; r is Pearson’s correlation coefficient. (c) H3K4me1 snCUT&Tag UMAPs from tumors 15 and 18 (Fig. 3e), colored by CyTOF-derived labels (top), with predicted-label composition per snCUT&Tag cluster (middle) and UCell scores for the ‘Down in Luminal vs. Basal (Charafe)’ signature (bottom). (d) Cells were classified as luminal or basal-like by CyTOF label transfer as in c. Differences in mean UCell scores for the indicated signatures between basal-like and luminal cells are shown across three tumors. EMT and basal-like-associated gene signatures show higher H3K4me1 deposition in the CyTOF-predicted basal-like group. (e) K5High and K5Low sorted cell populations from the luminal PDX model or MCF7 cells were subjected to H3K4me1 CUT&Tag. Peaks unique to each population were assigned to genes and compared to the indicated gene signatures. Shown is the difference in the GeneRatio (overlap count divided by the total number of peak-associated genes in that population) for each population, with positive values indicating increased overlap in K5High (basal-like) cells, whereas negative values indicate increased overlap in K5Low (luminal) cells. (f) Tumor 8 H3K9me2 snCUT&Tag UMAP from a 20kb-bin matrix, clustered by Leiden clustering (left). Stroma percentages per cluster, based on the H3K4me1-trained classifier, are shown on the right. (g) Following removal of the stromal compartment described in f, a normalized promoter-proximal H3K9me2 occupancy matrix was generated, and Leiden clustering was applied (n = 4,419 cells, see Methods). (h) Percentage of basal-like cells (cluster 2 in Fig. 3e) within each cluster in g, based on the H3K4me1-trained classifier. (i) Left: Differentially H3K9me2-bound genes in cluster 4, shown in g (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, log2FC > 0.6, adjusted p-value < 0.01), were tested against MSigDB Hallmark and Breast-related signatures. Shown are the top 5 terms significantly enriched (nominal p-value < 0.05) for genes with upregulation of H3K9me2 on their promoters. Right: UMAP as in g colored according to UCell gene-signature scores for the indicated gene sets. Cluster 4 shows elevated H3K9me2 occupancy over luminal-associated genes. (j) Read count per cell (nCount) by cluster (panel g). Violin plots show the distribution of individual cells, with the median denoted by a white dot and n indicated for each cluster. Cluster 4 shows the highest number of reads per cell, possibly corresponding to higher global levels of this mark in basal-like cells.

(a,b) Classifier performance in an independently processed, batch-corrected cohort of healthy individuals (n = 19) and luminal BC patients (n = 30), using the model trained on the original cohort in Fig. 4f. (a) ROC curve (AUC = 0.98; shading, 95% CI). (b) Confusion matrix with specificity set to 0.9. (c,d) ROC curve discriminating healthy individuals (n = 32) from luminal BC patients, diagnosed at the SHEBA medical center, Israel (c, n = 16, AUC = 0.96) or Kaplan medical center, Israel (d, n = 14, AUC = 0.99). Shading indicates the 95% CI. (e) ROC curve discriminating healthy individuals (n = 32) and triple-negative BC patients (n = 22, AUC = 0.98, shading indicates the 95% CI). (f) Healthy (n = 51) and luminal BC samples from three medical centers (n = 137) were pooled and stratified into 75% training cohort and a 25% test cohort. ROC curves are shown for training (left, n = 38 healthy vs. 103 luminal BC samples, AUC = 0.96) and the test cohort (right, n = 13 healthy vs. 34 luminal BC patients, AUC = 0.94). Shading indicates the 95% CI. (g) AUC estimates for discrimination of healthy individuals (n = 51) from luminal A (n = 98), luminal B (n = 31), or all luminal BC patients (n = 137) across the three medical centers. Points and lines indicate AUCs and 95% CIs, respectively.

Two-sided Wilcoxon tests. (g) Distribution of 29 EPINUC features across luminal BC patients stratified by histological grade (grade 1, n = 29; grade 2, n = 67; grade 3, n = 36). Points represent individual patients. Kruskal-Wallis p-values were Benjamini-Hochberg-corrected across the 29 features. (h) Spearman correlations between mean histone PTM levels measured by CyTOF in tumor cells and EPINUC measurements in matched plasma (n = 10). Correlations with r > 0.2 are pink; P < 0.05 is bold (two-sided Spearman correlation test). H3K4me3 and H3K27me3 scatter plots are shown below, with Theil-Sen fits and 95% CIs. (i) Individual PPS analysis distinguishing disease-free (DF) from relapse (R, left column), or between healthy individuals (H) and each of the luminal outcome group. Color indicates PPS, reflecting predictive power of each individual feature. (j) OncotypeDX scores for patients in cohorts MAYO-1 and MAYO-2 with available measurements (disease-free, n = 40; relapse, n = 9, n.s., non-significant, two-sided Wilcoxon test). In a–g,j, boxes show median and 25th–75th percentiles; whiskers extend to the largest/smallest value within 1.5×IQR.

Manchester United have officially confirmed an agreement to hire Mauricio Pochettino as their new manager to replace Michael Carrick.

Carrick’s sacking was announced yesterday, and now Man Utd have provided a further update by confirming that Pochettino will be their new manager with immediate effect.

The former Tottenham and Chelsea manager is leaving his role as head coach of the United States Men’s National Team to take over at Old Trafford, and the club praised him in their official statement.

“The Argentinian is renowned for his high-intensity, attacking style of football, his dedication to building strong, cohesive teams and his outstanding record of developing individual players,” United said on their website.

“Pochettino has consistently performed at the highest level of football across multiple leagues. He began his coaching career with Espanyol in 2009 before joining Southampton and achieving a club-record Premier League points tally in 2014.

“During five full seasons at Tottenham Hotspur, Pochettino established the club as regular UEFA Champions League contenders, securing qualification in four consecutive seasons and leading the club to its first final in the competition in 2019.

“In 2021, he joined Paris Saint-Germain, where he won the Ligue 1 title, the Coupe de France and the Trophée des Champions before joining Chelsea in 2023.”

Pochettino’s work at Spurs really stands out in his career so far, where he managed to make the club more competitive than they’ve ever been in the modern era.

The 54-year-old also achieved that without requiring huge amounts of money to spend, instead working with top young talents and helping them develop into superstars, most notably Harry Kane and Son Heung-min.

It will be interesting to see if Pochettino can now have better luck at turning things around for MUFC after a bit of a dismal recent period.

More Stories / Latest News Man United considering signing Argentine talent for key role in Pochettino’s squad Nov 13 2026, 11:41 Bruno Fernandes rejects Man Utd deal – Pochettino arrival makes his replacement obvious Nov 13 2026, 11:05 Leeds United expected to be in race to sign “top-class striker” Nov 13 2026, 9:24

Carrick started well as interim manager, but perhaps lacked the experience to take on such a challenging job permanently.

That shouldn’t be a problem with Pochettino, who has managed at the very highest level consistently for more than a decade now.

Read more here for the signing Pochettino needs to get his United project off to the perfect start!

#1328. Former Old Firm rivals reveal how clubs walked a fine line between rivalry and respect...and even stopped by for tea and sympathy in times of trouble!

Published: 12:20 EST, 13 November 2026 | Updated: 12:29 EST, 13 November 2026

They have reached an age when they would once have been categorised as the old infirm. Yet in the autumn of 2026 they cavort around Toryglen with an almost juvenile vigour.

They have reached the age when they can reflect on being stalwarts of the Old Firm. Yet they are outlining plans and strategy for a vital, growing movement.

The two meetings are separated by two sets of stairs. On the ground level, men of pensionable age and beyond play walking football. Just above sit Campbell Ogilvie, former secretary of Rangers and president of the Scottish FA, and Eric Riley, once company secretary and director of Celtic.

They are both on the board of Walking Football Scotland, an organisation that now has more than 5,000 people playing the game across 160 clubs, with participants ranging from 40 to 93.

The venerable statesmen of the Scottish game may be perceived to be rivals, but only in matters on the pitch. They sit in an office in the south side of Glasgow and reminisce about how they first met 50 years ago when playing five-a-sides and then renewed that rivalry in their professional life.

As the Glasgow rivals now seem regularly at odds, both men recalled a time when friendship was paramount amid the sporting mayhem.

Former Rangers secretary Campbell Ogilvie and ex-Celtic director Eric Riley are firm friends

‘The two clubs always had a good relationship back in those days,’ said Ogilvie, now 76 and still playing football. ‘We wanted to beat each other — naturally. But off the field we had a very close relationship.’

He told a remarkable story that backs that assertion.

‘There was one day I was at Ibrox in the early 1980s when the team was not doing so well. The phone rang and it was Sean Fallon, Jock Stein’s former Celtic assistant. I had known Sean from my days with the Scottish League and he said: “I know you’re going through a rocky spell, so I’m coming over for a cup of tea”.

‘Over he comes. So there was a very close relationship in those days. I’m not there now and for all I know there still is. But certainly, when I was there and Eric was at Celtic, we could talk to each other.’

Riley, 69, agreed: ‘Absolutely. John McClelland (former Rangers chairman) was one we could talk to. And Martin (Bain, former chief executive) I suppose, when he came along a bit later. Between myself and Peter Lawwell (former Celtic chief executive and chairman) the relationship between the clubs off the field was actually quite strong. But on the field we still wanted to win.’

Ogilvie added: ‘There was a respect. And I go back to the Willie Waddells and the Willie Thorntons, there was that respect. More recently that was there with the likes of Jack McGinn and so on.

‘We had a good relationship but it’s fair to say that there was no social media in those days. You know all the toxic stuff that can bring.’

The traits of respect and sporting competitiveness have been obvious in both men since they first met half a century ago. ‘We played five-a-side football at Scotstoun before the football careers started. It was just casual games,’ said Ogilvie. ‘We were in our early 20s. Eric was an accountant and I think those games were arranged through accountants.

‘I played youth football when I was 16 and, 60 years down the line, playing football is still a major part of my life.’

Ogilvie began walking football eight years ago and Riley soon after. ‘I suffer from Parkinson’s, amongst other things,’ said Riley. ‘I was getting assistance through Stobhill Hospital and the physiotherapist there, who specialises in Parkinson’s patients, got in touch to say there was a project going on at Toryglen where they were playing walking football and assessing you to see what the benefits may or may not be.’

Ogilvie and Riley are both on the board of Walking Football and have played a big role in its rise

Riley agreed to take part. ‘I really enjoyed it because you are back playing football again, you have the camaraderie and you have the home baking which I never really get at home.’

Riley had a hip replacement in March and admitted: ‘I have not played since then. I miss it. I play a few other things which are more and more difficult. I play tennis.’

His tennis history is illustrious as he played with Judy Murray in Scottish championships. ‘She went off to the tour and I went off to university,’ says Riley. He is unstinting in his praise of the woman who became the mother of the No1 in men’s singles and men’s doubles.

The repartee between Riley and Ogilvie is relaxed but both men have a resolve to grow walking football. Their task has been helped by bookmakers William Hill stepping in with sponsorship.

The benefits of the sport stretch beyond the physical. Ogilvie gave his own experience.

‘When you have finished working, there is a void, not mixing with people, not being with people, and walking football certainly has helped me fill that. Hopefully it helps me keep a bit fitter too,’ he said.

Ogilvie pointed out: ‘The issues you tend to encounter are health. Grief is another one. There are quite a few of the guys who have lost their wives and quite a few who are just sitting on the sofa watching Homes Under the Hammer.’

Walking football, too, has attracted a large cadre of women. ‘One of the things that stood out for me was the number of females playing,’ said Riley. ‘I went along to my first session and there were four female players, three of whom had never kicked a football in their life previously. Walking football got them involved and they really enjoyed it.’

Walking football has made giant leaps in Scotland but the next step is to collate data so cases for funding will be made unanswerable.

‘We need facts or what is called data,’ said Ogilvie. ‘We are trying to do some studies with universities to get that data — physical and mental — and get it to the government. We want to prove the benefits and then we could make this prescriptive through surgeries.

‘We see the benefits day to day anecdotally but that doesn’t bring you the data. Sponsorship helps.

Walking Football attracts thousands of participants at clubs across the country

‘The university studies won’t come overnight because they need to be detailed. But if we could get to the stage where we could prove the benefits, then the NHS and the government would see that proof in black and white.’

This is all serious and proper. But both men were keen to emphasise that the game was fun. Ogilvie said: ‘When I started, I asked someone: “How would you sum up walking football?” He said to me: “It’s a cross between watching Barcelona and the Gurkha warriors”.’

He added: ‘I loved when at the end of an over-75s tournament one player said to another: “Good game, son”.’

The football world has thus moved into a new era. But some things cannot change. Ogilvie said: ‘One of my grandsons, who is 10, came along to watch a session and said two things. Firstly, it is a bit more intense than he thought and second there are no pink boots.’

Riley chimed in: ‘That would be an affront, that would be unacceptable.’

Even in walking football some things are a step too far.

■ Eric Riley and Campbell Ogilvie were speaking at the announcement of William Hill as official sponsor of Walking Football Scotland. To find your nearest game visit walkingfootballscotland.org

Liverpool defender Virgil van Dijk is reportedly attracting interest from AC Milan and Juventus as he heads towards the end of his contract.

The Netherlands international is facing an uncertain few months ahead as he will be out of contract at Anfield in summer 2027, meaning he can start negotiating with overseas clubs from January.

According to BBC Sport, this has both Milan and Juve on alert and monitoring Van Dijk’s situation, while there’s also the suggestion of interest from Turkish clubs.

Van Dijk has had a tremendous career at Liverpool, but he’s 35 now and will be 36 by the start of next season, so it might be time for the Reds to start thinking about bringing in a long-term replacement.

As reported via the Daily Briefing, our understanding is that Brighton’s talented young Croatian centre-back Luka Vuskovic is seen as a highly-regarded option for that role.

Van Dijk and Liverpool have a big decision to make, with the former Southampton man likely to want to keep on playing regularly at the highest level for a bit longer.

We’re increasingly seeing top players carry on into their late 30s and even early 40s in the case of some high-profile stars like Cristiano Ronaldo, Luka Modric, and Thiago Silva.

Want more CaughtOffside coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust

Van Dijk may well feel he could replicate that, but he’s more likely to do so if he steps down to a slightly less competitive level.

The slower pace of the game in Italian football could therefore be ideal for Van Dijk at this stage of his career, though if he is able to carry on performing well for a year or two more, then there’s no reason for LFC to push him out.
